topic:overview:why:body: Agriculture covers 40% of U.S. land and accounts for approximately 80% of consumptive water use. However these impacts are large due to the scale of production. U.S. farmers produce more than any other country besides India and China and twice as much as they did in 1970. Without efficiency improvements, this level of production would have far larger impacts.
topic:overview:happened:body: Following a trajectory of sustainable intensification, the environmental intensity of agriculture—the resource use or environmental impacts per unit of production—has fallen nearly across the board. Since 1990, farm output rose more than 50% while greenhouse gas emissions rose only 8 percent and land use and water withdrawals both fell.  In some cases total impacts have declined; in others rising impacts have been far outpaced by increasing production.
topic:overview:chart:0:title: Agricultural output, resource use, and impacts
topic:nitrogen:happened:body: Nitrogen surplus—the nitrogen added to cropland but not removed in crops—rose sharply through the 1970s before plateauing. Nitrogen-use efficiency, the share of nitrogen taken up by crops, started to reach over 70% in 2016. This has helped shrink the Gulf dead zone, though it is still larger than EPA's goal.

topic:nitrogen:why:body: Nitrogen not taken up by crops can contribute to nitrous oxide emissions, drinking-water contamination, and algal blooms. In the Gulf, nutrient-fueled blooms can drain oxygen from bottom waters, creating a summer dead zone where aquatic life struggles to survive.
topic:water:title: With better irrigation, water use plateaued
topic:water:happened:body: Irrigation and livestock withdrawals rose until 1980 before plateauing and falling. As agricultural output grew, withdrawals per unit of farm output fell by more than half. Yet regional challenges persist, with High Plains aquifer levels still falling.
study:water:description: Volume of water use per unit of product.
topic:soil:why:body: Erosion removes fertile topsoil, carries sediment and nutrients into waterways, and can undermine long-term productivity. Keeping soil in place supports both yields and water quality.
topic:practices:chart:1:subtitle: Less disturbance and more winter cover help curb erosion, retain moisture, and protect yield potential.

topic:rd:happened:body: From its peak in 2002 until 2024, R&D funding and spending fell 26 percent (inflation-adjusted). R&D intensity—spending as a percent of the sector's value—has fallen even more: about 45% since 2002. Agricultural productivity growth has subsequently slowed, though it is influenced by other factors too.
topic:climate:happened:body: Direct U.S. agricultural emissions were 595 million metric tons CO₂e in 2023, 8 percent above 1990. Estimates by economic sector, which includes on-farm fuel use, are higher. Yet emissions would be higher still without the dramatic reductions seen in emissions intensity, e.g., per lb or bushel.
topic:nitrogen:title: Efficiency improvements help shrink Dead Zone
topic:herbicides:happened:body: From the early 1990s to 2015, acute toxicity quotients declined for four of the five crops studied, while chronic hazard quotients declined for two. Much of the acute improvement came as hazardous products like alachlor and cyanazine were phased out.
topic:soil:happened:body: Conservation tillage, cover cropping, contour farming, and related practices helped lower both water and wind erosion. Most of the national improvement occurred in the 80s and 90s, with erosion rates since leveling off.

topic:rd:why:body: Public agricultural research is the largest driver of productivity growth, improving yields, resource efficiency,  and environmental performance. Since its benefits can take decades to emerge, sustained investment is critical.

topic:livestock:why:body: Selective breeding, better nutrition and feeding, disease control, improved housing, and mechanization help producers obtain more output from feed and animals. Larger and more specialized operations make some of these practices easier to use. These shifts, in turn, cut the  environmental footprint of each major livestock product,
topic:livestock:happened:body: Broilers need much less feed per pound while reaching heavier weights at younger ages. Pig litters have grown. And dairies have widely adopted productivity-enhancing technologies, particularly automation.
